questions.q: Diarrhea is defined as stool water content >____ mL/24 hours.
questions.exp: Definition: Stool water content >200 mL/24 hours. (Book p1)

questions.q: Match the Bristol stool types to the book's clinical label — 1) Type 1 & 2 2) Type 3 & 4 3) Type 6 & 7 … A) Normal B) Constipation C) Diarrhea
questions.exp: According to Bristol stool chart: Type 1 & 2 = Constipation, Type 6 & 7 = Diarrhea; Types 3-4 are Normal. (Book p1)

questions.q: Bristol Type 1 is described as separate hard lumps and is labelled as:
questions.exp: Type 1: Separate hard lumps = SEVERE CONSTIPATION on the Bristol chart. (Book p1)

questions.q: Bristol Type 2 (lumpy and sausage like) corresponds to:
questions.exp: Type 2: Lumpy and sausage like = MILD CONSTIPATION. (Book p1)

questions.q: Bristol Type 3 – ‘A sausage shape with cracks in the surface’ – is classified as:
questions.exp: Type 3: A sausage shape with cracks in the surface = NORMAL. (Book p1)

questions.q: Bristol Type 4 – ‘Like a smooth, soft sausage or snake’ – is:
questions.exp: Type 4: Like a smooth, soft sausage or snake = NORMAL. (Book p1)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one pairing is NOT as printed for the Bristol chart:
opts: Type 5 – Soft blobs with clear-cut edges – LACKING FIBRE
Type 6 – Mushy consistency with ragged edges – MILD DIARRHEA
Type 7 – Liquid consistency with no solid pieces – SEVERE DIARRHEA
Type 5 – Soft blobs with clear-cut edges – SEVERE CONSTIPATION
questions.exp: Type 5 is Soft blobs with clear-cut edges = LACKING FIBRE, not severe constipation; the other three are as printed. (Book p1)

questions.q: Bristol Type 5 (soft blobs with clear-cut edges) is labelled ____.
questions.exp: Type 5: Soft blobs with clear-cut edges = LACKING FIBRE. (Book p1)

questions.q: Bristol Type 6 – mushy consistency with ragged edges – indicates:
questions.exp: Type 6: Mushy consistency with ragged edges = MILD DIARRHEA. (Book p1)

questions.q: A patient reports stools that are entirely liquid with no solid pieces. By Bristol chart this is Type 7 and the book labels it:
questions.exp: Type 7: Liquid consistency with no solid pieces = SEVERE DIARRHEA. (Book p1)

questions.q: Match the phases of absorption as book-ordered — 1) Luminal 2) Mucosal 3) Post mucosal … A) Post mucosal B) Luminal C) Mucosal
questions.exp: Physiology of absorption: 1. Luminal, 2. Mucosal, 3. Post mucosal. (Book p1)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — the book states that the mucosal phase occurs mainly in the small intestine and accounts for maximum absorption.
opts: True — but post mucosal is majority
questions.exp: Mucosal: Small intestine (majority), maximum absorption. (Book p1)

questions.q: Among macronutrients listed, which is noted as most calorie-dense?
questions.exp: Fat: most calorie dense nutrient. (Book p1)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — fat is the most specific nutrient affected in malabsorption.
opts: True — fat is the most specific marker
True — but only in pancreatic insufficiency
questions.exp: Fat: most specific nutrient affected in malabsorption. (Book p1)

questions.q: Three are listed under ‘macronutrients for absorption’ in the book. Pick the ODD ONE OUT:
questions.exp: The book lists Fat, Carbohydrates, Proteins under macronutrients; Vitamins is not listed there. (Book p1)

questions.q: By Frequency Classification, ‘Acute’ diarrhea is defined as duration:
questions.exp: Frequency Classification: Acute <2 weeks (Nuisance symptom). (Book p1)

questions.q: Match the frequency label to duration — 1) Acute 2) Persistent 3) Chronic … A) >4 weeks B) <2 weeks C) >2 weeks
questions.exp: Acute <2 weeks, Persistent >2 weeks, Chronic >4 weeks. (Book p1)

questions.q: The most common cause of acute diarrhea overall, per the book, is:
questions.exp: Acute diarrhea: Infectious: Viral infection (m/c). (Book p1)

questions.q: A 28-year-old food handler develops acute watery diarrhea for 12 hours after a buffet; no blood. The book’s most common viral cause in adults is:
questions.exp: m/c in adults: Norovirus. (Book p1)

questions.q: A 2-year-old with acute watery diarrhea, low-grade fever, self-limited course. The book’s most common viral cause in children is:
questions.exp: m/c in children: Rotavirus. (Book p1)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — acute viral diarrhea as described is typically self-limiting.
questions.exp: Acute viral diarrhea is listed as Self-limiting. (Book p1)

questions.q: Match chronic diarrhea D/d to etiology — 1) Osmotic 2) Secretory 3) Inflammatory … A) Inflammatory bowel disease B) Malabsorption C) Tumor / Toxin
questions.exp: Chronic diarrhea table: Osmotic → malabsorption, Secretory → Tumor/Toxin, Inflammatory → Inflammatory bowel disease. (Book p2)

questions.q: Malassimilation = ____ + malabsorption.
questions.exp: Malassimilation: maldigestion + malabsorption. (Book p2)

questions.q: Malassimilation is diminished intestinal digestion/absorption of ____.
questions.exp: Diminished intestinal digestion/absorption of one or more nutrients. (Book p2)

questions.q: Which is described as the most consistent clinical symptom of malabsorption under Pathological Classification?
questions.exp: 1. OSMOTIC DIARRHEA — most consistent clinical symptom of malabsorption. (Book p2)

questions.q: A patient passes pale, bulky, fatty, malodorous, greasy stools that float. The book terms this hallmark of malabsorption as:
questions.exp: Steatorrhea: Hallmark of malabsorption. Definition: Passing of pale, bulky, fatty, malodorous, greasy stools. (Book p2)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — the book lists diarrhea as the most consistent clinical finding in steatorrhea.
opts: False — weight loss is most consistent
False — steatorrhea is always painless so diarrhea is rare
questions.exp: Clinical presentation: Diarrhea (most consistent clinical finding) in steatorrhea. (Book p2)

questions.q: Order the osmotic diarrhea pathogenesis as printed — 1) ↓ Fat absorption in small intestine 2) Unabsorbed macronutrients ↑ stool osmolality (osmotically active) in colon 3) Stool draws water from large intestinal epithelial cells … A) Stool draws water B) ↓ Fat absorption C) ↑ Stool osmolality
questions.exp: Pathology: ↓ fat absorption in small intestine → In colon → Unabsorbed macronutrients ↑ stool osmolality (osmotically active) → Stool draws water from large intestinal epithelial cells → Osmotic diarrhea. (Book p2)

questions.q: Gold standard investigation for steatorrhea per the book is:
questions.exp: Investigations: 1. 72 hour fecal fat test: Gold standard. (Book p2)

questions.q: For the 72-hour fecal fat test, the book’s prescribed fat input is:
questions.exp: Procedure: Fat input = 100 g/day. (Book p2)

questions.q: Normal fecal fat excretion on the 72-hour test is:
questions.exp: Normal: <7 g/day. (Book p2)

questions.q: Steatorrhea is diagnosed if fecal fat is >7 g/day for 3 days on ____.
questions.exp: >7 g/day for 3 days (D3, D4, D5) = Steatorrhea. (Book p2)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — stool fat excretion ≥7% also qualifies as steatorrhea by the book’s criteria.
opts: True — but only with Sudan stain
questions.exp: Stool fat excretion ≥7% → Steatorrhea. (Book p2)

questions.q: Match the qualitative stool fat test to its stain — 1) Sudan III 2) Sudan IV 3) Oil red O … A) Oil red O B) Sudan III C) Sudan IV
questions.exp: Qualitative stool fat: Sudan III, Sudan IV, Oil red O. (Book p2)

questions.q: Which pair is listed under toxins causing secretory diarrhea?
questions.exp: Secretory: a. Toxins → ETEC, V. cholera (heat labile toxin). (Book p3)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — enteropathogenic virus (rotavirus) is listed under secretory diarrhea toxin etiology.
opts: True — listed as toxin-mediated secretory cause
questions.exp: Toxins → Enteropathogenic virus (rotavirus) is listed. (Book p3)

questions.q: A patient with chronic watery diarrhea, hypokalemia and non-anion gap acidosis with a pancreatic tumor is described. The book’s tumor and triad are:
opts: VIPoma with WDHA (Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, Acidosis)
questions.exp: Tumours: VIPoma → Watery Diarrhoea → WDHA syndrome with Hypokalemia and Acidosis triangle. (Book p3)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — in secretory diarrhea the book notes ‘No structural damage seen.’
questions.exp: Note: No structural damage seen (secretory diarrhea). (Book p3)

questions.q: Match the stool osmotic gap category — 1) Osmotic diarrhea 2) Secretory diarrhea … A) Normal/decreased (<50 mOsm/kg), ↑ stool Na⁺+K⁺ B) Increased (>100 mOsm/kg)
questions.exp: Stool osmotic gap: Osmotic Increased (>100), Secretory Normal/decreased (<50), ↑ stool Na+ + K+ (By toxins). (Book p3)

questions.q: A patient’s diarrhea improves dramatically on fasting. The comparison table suggests:
questions.exp: Response to fasting: Osmotic → Improvement, Secretory → No change. (Book p3)

questions.q: Osmotic diarrhea stool pH is typically <5.5 due to fermentation of unabsorbed carbohydrates to acids; secretory diarrhea stool pH is:
questions.exp: Stool pH: Osmotic <5.5 (Fermentation… → Acids), Secretory >6.0. (Book p3)

questions.q: Stool osmotic gap = 290 − 2 × (stool ____ + stool ____).
questions.exp: Note: Stool osmotic gap = measured osmolality - calculated; 290 - 2 (Stool Na⁺ + K⁺). (Book p3)

questions.q: Normal stool osmotic gap is:
questions.exp: Normal: 50-100 mOsm/kg. (Book p3)

questions.q: An adolescent female with chronic diarrhea, no weight gain, fatigue, and normal supervised stool osmolality but very low unsupervised osmolality. The book’s clinical picture fits:
questions.exp: Factitious: Adolescent female, Chronic diarrhea, Fatigue, Weight loss. (Book p3)

questions.q: In factitious diarrhea findings, unsupervised stool (mixed with water) osmolality is about ____, supervised is about 279.
questions.exp: Unsupervised (mixed with water) Very low (~16 mOsm/kg), Supervised Normal (~279). (Book p4)

questions.q: Match etiology to site in Anatomical Classification — 1) Osmotic/Secretory (ETEC, Vibrio cholera) 2) Invasive organisms (Shigella) / Ulcerative colitis inflammation … A) Large intestinal diarrhea B) Small intestinal diarrhea
questions.exp: Small intestinal: Osmotic, Secretory - ETEC, Vibrio cholera; Large intestinal: Invasive (Shigella), Inflammation: ulcerative colitis. (Book p4)

questions.q: By the Small vs Large table, stool volume is:
opts: Large in small intestinal (↓ nutrient absorption) vs Small in large intestinal
Small in small intestinal vs Large in large intestinal
questions.exp: Clinical presentation: Volume - Large (↓ nutrient absorption) in small intestinal, Small in large intestinal. (Book p4)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — both small and large intestinal diarrheas are listed as ‘watery’ in consistency per the table.
opts: True — both are listed as watery
questions.exp: Consistency: Small → watery, Large → watery. (Book p4)

questions.q: Frequency/urgency in the anatomical table is:
opts: ↓ in small intestinal, ↑ in large intestinal
questions.exp: Frequency/urgency: Small ↓, Large ↑. (Book p4)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — pus/blood/mucus is Absent in small intestinal diarrhea and Present in large intestinal diarrhea.
questions.exp: Pus/blood/mucus: Small Absent, Large Present. (Book p4)

questions.q: Tenesmus is:
opts: Present in small, Absent in large
Absent in small, Present in large
questions.exp: Tenesmus: Small Absent, Large Present. (Book p4)

questions.q: Dyschezia is:
opts: Absent in small intestinal, Present in large intestinal
Present in small, Absent in large
questions.exp: Dyschezia: Small Absent, Large Present. (Book p4)

questions.q: Abdominal pain is:
opts: Absent in small intestinal, Present in large intestinal
Present in small, Absent in large
questions.exp: Abdominal pain: Small Absent, Large Present. (Book p4)

questions.q: Fever is:
opts: Absent in small intestinal diarrhea, Present in large intestinal diarrhea
Present in small, Absent in large
questions.exp: Fever: Small Absent, Large Present. (Book p4)

questions.q: Three are Present in both small and large intestinal diarrhea; pick the ODD ONE OUT that is NOT present in both:
opts: Abdominal cramps and Bloating are both Present
questions.exp: Abdominal cramps: Present in both; Bloating: Present in both; Fever: Absent in small, Present in large — so fever is the odd one. (Book p4)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — bloating is Present in both small and large intestinal diarrhea.
questions.exp: Bloating: Present in both. (Book p4)

questions.q: A patient with chronic large volume diarrhea for 6 months has lost 8 kg; vomiting is occasional. The table suggests this fits:
opts: Small intestinal diarrhea (weight loss Present if persistent, vomiting maybe present, steatorrhoea Present)
questions.exp: Weight loss: Small intestinal Present (if persistent), Large Rare; Vomiting maybe present in small, Rare in large; Steatorrhoea Present in small, Absent in large. (Book p4)

questions.q: Vomiting in the anatomical classification is:
opts: Maybe present in small intestinal, Rare in large intestinal
Rare in small, Maybe present in large
questions.exp: Vomiting: Small maybe present, Large Rare. (Book p4)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — steatorrhoea is Present in small intestinal diarrhea and Absent in large intestinal diarrhea.
questions.exp: Steatorrhoea: Small Present, Large Absent. (Book p4)

questions.q: By ‘Approach to Diarrhea’ flowchart, diarrhea <2 weeks suggests:
questions.exp: Duration <2 weeks → Infection. (Book p5)

questions.q: Match the <2 weeks infection by site — 1) Small intestine (Large volume): Viral m/c, ETEC, Cholera 2) Large intestine (Fever, pain abdomen, blood, mucus) … A) Invasive: Shigella, Non-typhoid salmonella, Campylobacter B) Viral m/c, ETEC, Cholera (Self limiting)
questions.exp: <2 weeks: Small intestine (Large volume): Viral m/c, ETEC, Cholera → Self limiting; Large intestine (Fever, pain, blood, mucus): Invasive: Shigella, Non typhoid salmonella, Campylobacter. (Book p5)

questions.q: A traveler with 1-day history of large volume watery diarrhea, no fever/blood, likely viral/ETEC/cholera. The book’s flowchart implies:
questions.exp: Small intestine viral/ETEC/Cholera → Self limiting. (Book p5)

questions.q: For diarrhea >4 weeks, match — 1) Small intestine - Osmotic 2) Small intestine - Secretory 3) Large intestine - Inflammatory … A) VIPoma B) ↑ stool osmotic gap, Improves on fasting C) Ulcerative colitis
questions.exp: >4 weeks: Small → Osmotic: ↑ stool osmotic gap, Improves on fasting; Secretory: VIPoma; Large → Inflammatory: ulcerative colitis. (Book p5)

questions.q: A patient has chronic watery diarrhea for 6 weeks with hypokalemia. Fasting does NOT improve stool output. Workup for VIPoma is planned. This matches which branch of the approach flowchart?
opts: Small intestinal osmotic (>100 gap, improves on fasting)
Small intestinal secretory (VIPoma, no improvement on fasting)
questions.exp: Small intestinal Secretory: VIPoma (diarrhea persists fasting) vs Osmotic: ↑ gap, Improves on fasting. (Book p5)

questions.q: A patient has >4 weeks diarrhea with fever, abdominal pain, blood/mucus, urgency, and tenesmus. Approach flowchart points to:
opts: Small intestinal osmotic with lactase deficiency
questions.exp: Large intestine >4 weeks → Inflammatory: ulcerative colitis (presents with Fever, pain abdomen, blood, mucus). (Book p5)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — not listed under invasive organisms for Large intestinal <2 weeks infection:
questions.exp: Invasive organisms for Large intestine: Shigella, Non typhoid salmonella, Campylobacter; ETEC is Small intestinal (Large volume). (Book p5)

units.title: Definition & Bristol Chart
units.guide:
Definition >200 mL/24 h and Bristol Types 1-7.
Link Type numbers to stool form and clinical label.
Severe constipation (1) through severe diarrhea (7) in strict order.

units.title: Physiology & Macronutrients
units.guide:
Luminal → Mucosal (small intestine, maximum) → Post mucosal.
Fat is most calorie-dense and most specific in malabsorption.
List carbs and proteins as the other macronutrients.

units.title: Frequency Classification & Acute Etiology
units.guide:
Acute <2w (nuisance), Persistent >2w, Chronic >4w.
Acute viral m/c overall: Norovirus adults, Rotavirus children, self-limiting.
Classify by duration first in the flowchart.

units.title: Chronic Diarrhea & Malassimilation
units.guide:
Chronic D/d: Osmotic→malabsorption, Secretory→tumor/toxin, Inflammatory→IBD.
Malassimilation = maldigestion + malabsorption.
Diminished digestion/absorption of one or more nutrients.

units.title: Osmotic Diarrhea & Steatorrhea
units.guide:
Osmotic = most consistent symptom of malabsorption.
Steatorrhea = hallmark: pale bulky fatty malodorous greasy stools.
Pathology: ↓ fat absorption → ↑ stool osmolality → draws water → osmotic diarrhea.

units.title: Steatorrhea Investigations
units.guide:
72-h fecal fat = gold standard with 100 g/day fat input.
Normal <7 g/day; steatorrhea >7 g/d for 3 d (D3-D5) or ≥7% excretion.
Qualitative: Sudan III, Sudan IV, Oil red O.

units.title: Secretory Diarrhea & Stool Osmotic Gap
units.guide:
Secretory: ETEC/V. cholera heat-labile toxin + rotavirus; VIPoma→WDHA + hypoK + acidosis; no structural damage.
Gap table: Osmotic >100 + pH<5.5 vs Secretory <50 + ↑Na+K + pH>6.0 + no change on fasting.
Formula 290−2(Na⁺+K⁺), normal 50-100; factitious case adolescent female.

units.title: Factitious & Anatomical Classification
units.guide:
Factitious unsupervised ~16 vs supervised ~279.
Small vs Large etiology + full clinical table (volume, consistency, frequency, pus/blood/mucus, tenesmus, dyschezia, pain, fever, cramps, bloating, weight loss, vomiting, steatorrhoea) in order.
Weight loss/vomiting/steatorrhoea distinguish persistent small intestinal.

units.title: Approach to Diarrhea
units.guide:
Duration first: <2w = infection, >4w = small vs large.
<2w Small (large volume, viral/ETEC/cholera, self-limiting) vs Large (fever/pain/blood, Shigella etc).
>4w Small osmotic (>100 gap, improves) vs secretory (VIPoma) vs Large inflammatory (UC).
